lesson_title: A Weather Report the Size of a Button
hook_text: This tiny circle knows tomorrow's weather. Here's how to read it.
clip_script: Each small circle on a weather chart is a whole report folded to the size of a shirt button. Open one up. The circle is the sky itself: slice the sky into eight pieces like a milk tart and count the cloudy slices — ours shows seven of eight shaded, a low grey lid with one strip of blue left. The upper-left number is the temperature: 21 degrees. The number under it, 18, is the dew point — a moisture gauge in disguise. Never ask what the dew point is; ask how far it sits from the temperature. Ours are three degrees apart: three small degrees of cooling and this air starts turning to droplets. Thick, damp air with weather loading up. Last, the little feathered shaft flying into the circle. It flies in from the direction the wind comes from — ours from the north-west. The feathers give speed: a full feather is ten knots, a half is five — fifteen knots, washing-line weather. Warm, nearly saturated, sky closing, moist wind feeding in. Every reading agrees: something is coming. On a winter chart, that something is the cold front.
visual_style: A tiny station model zooming up from a national chart, each element lighting up and unfolding into its meaning — pie-slice sky, thermometer, narrowing gap meter, feathered wind arrow — before zooming back out to show an approaching toothed front line.
mood: Detective energy — cracking a code hidden in plain sight.
pacing: Quick zoom in, one crisp beat per symbol, accelerating to the closing verdict: something is coming.
call_to_action: Take the full lesson and read tomorrow's weather straight off today's chart.
